prime.problem: Performance engineering for LLM serving looks like a pile of unrelated tricks: kernels, KV cache, batching, quantization, sharding, routing. Without one quantity they all move, you can't tell which trick matters for a given deployment or how they combine.
prime.fits: This is the series map, read before perf-1 or after perf-7 as a recap. It builds on nothing except the idea that a GPU-hour has a price; every later course fills in one term of its formula.
expect: the latency SLO as the constraint
the lever ranking (batching, bytes per token, idle math, hardware)
prime.goal: Draw the whole series as one causal map from GPU price to $/token, place each of the eight courses on it, and explain why batching is the biggest lever and what stops you batching forever.

attend: Which term in the $/token formula does each course (perf-1 to perf-7) move, and which course moves the SLO constraint instead?
Why does going from batch 1 to batch 64 make tokens 39× cheaper when the step time only rises from 4.79 to 7.80 ms?
The lever table groups GQA and FP8 KV under "fewer bytes per token". Why do fewer bytes buy both more users and shorter steps?
Why does speculative decoding help at batch 1 but slow things down (0.70×) at batch 256?
Kernels and engines don't get their own row in the lever table. Why does the card treat them as a multiplier on every row instead?

must: Decode reads all 16.06 GB of weights per step whatever the batch → the weight read is shared by every user in the batch → tokens per step rises with B while T<sub>step</sub> rises only by the extra KV reads → tokens/s per GPU climbs → $/token falls (batch 1 → 64: $14.35 → $0.37)

Bigger batch → more KV reads per step → longer T<sub>step</sub> → slower tokens for each user (209 → 128 tok/s) → the latency SLO caps B → so every byte saved per token (GQA, FP8 KV, quantized weights) buys a bigger batch under the same SLO

Decode is memory-bound → the tensor cores sit mostly idle → spare math can verify guessed tokens (speculative decoding) → more tokens per weight read at small batch → but at large batch the math is no longer spare, so speculation costs more than it saves
The course formulas give theoretical floors → real kernels and engines reach only about half of them → kernel and engine work (perf-3, perf-5) is a multiplier on every lever, not a separate lever
elevated: Hardware choice for decode is really bandwidth per dollar → the same request drops from 970 ms on an H100 to 407 ms on a B200 because HBM goes 3.35 → 8.0 TB/s → compare chips on $/hr ÷ TB/s, not on FLOP/s
reference: the H100 list price $10.8/hr (GCP, Feb 2025) and that cloud prices vary
the lab tags [L] local Mac, [C] Colab T4, [H] rented H100

compress.prompt: Course-level compress: without looking, draw the whole series as one causal map. Start from "GPU $/hr" and end at "$ per million tokens", put B, T<sub>step</sub> and the SLO on it, and attach each of perf-1 to perf-7 to the box it changes.
checklist: $/M tokens = GPU $/hr ÷ (3600 × tokens/s) × 10<sup>6</sup>, and tokens/s = B ÷ T<sub>step</sub>
T<sub>step</sub> = KV reads + max(math, weight reads), bounded by the SLO
perf-1/perf-2 supply the arithmetic (FLOPs, bytes, B<sub>crit</sub>, KV per token, step time)
perf-3 kernels and perf-4 attention/KV shrink the time and bytes inside a step; perf-5 engines keep B high; perf-6 spreads a model across GPUs
perf-7 closes the loop: training cost upstream, $/token and hardware choice downstream
the constraint: bigger B lowers cost but slows each user

retrieve.q: Explain to a new colleague why an inference company's margin is set by tokens per GPU-second, and what single constraint stops them from simply maximising it.
answer: the GPU-hour is a fixed cost, so $/token = price ÷ tokens produced
every technique in the series raises tokens per GPU-second
the per-user latency SLO limits how large the batch (and so the step time) can get

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens to one decode step's time and to throughput when the batch goes from 1 to 64 users with 1,200-token contexts on Llama-3.1-8B/H100.
answer: weights read once either way: 16.06 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s = 4.79 ms
KV reads add 64 × 0.157 GB, so the step becomes 7.80 ms
math is only ~1 ms at batch 64, so the step stays memory-bound
tokens/s: 209 → 8,206 (39×); per user: 209 → 128 tok/s

retrieve.q: A product team wants the lowest possible per-token latency for a single premium user. Which levers from the ranking still help, which stop mattering, and what does the company pay?
answer: run at small batch, so the batching lever is given up deliberately
speculative decoding helps most here (209 → 468 tok/s at batch 1)
bandwidth per dollar and fewer weight bytes still shorten each step
the cost: many times more $ per token (batch 1 is $14.35/M vs $0.37 at batch 64)

retrieve.q: Place each of the eight courses on the $/token formula: which term does it change, and which course would you open first if a deployment's step time is fine but its batch stays small?
answer: perf-1/2: the arithmetic for every term
perf-3/4: shorter T<sub>step</sub> and fewer bytes per token
perf-5: keeps B high (scheduling, batching) and uses idle math (speculation)
perf-6: models bigger than one GPU; perf-7: price per hour and hardware choice
small batch with a fine step time → perf-5 (the scheduler) and the KV memory cards in perf-4

compare.q: This map's $/token formula vs perf-7's cost-per-token capstone: what does the capstone add that a floor-based formula leaves out, and when would the map's number mislead you?
answer: the map uses theoretical floors at 100% of peak bandwidth and FLOP/s
the capstone brings in real utilisation, engine overhead and hardware prices
the floor misleads when you compare it to a real bill: real systems reach roughly half the floor
both share the same structure: price ÷ tokens produced

compare.q: The map treats T<sub>step</sub> as one box; perf-2 derives it. What does the derivation reveal that the box hides, and which lever in the ranking depends on that detail?
answer: T<sub>step</sub> = KV reads + max(weight math, weight reads)
KV reads can't be shared across a batch, unlike the weight read
so the batching lever eventually hits a wall from KV bytes, which is why GQA and FP8 KV rank next
the map's box hides which term dominates at a given batch and context

compare.q: The overview organises the field by levers on one formula; the stack card organises it by layers a request passes through. When is each view the right one to reach for?
answer: levers: deciding what to optimise next and estimating its payoff
layers: finding who owns a component and where a request spends time
the same technique appears in both (batching = a lever and the layer-4 scheduler)
neither alone tells you whether a change is worth making AND where to make it

predict.q: Keep Llama-3.1-8B on one H100 at $10.8/hr and 1,200-token contexts, but run batch 16 instead of 64. Before computing: will the cost per million tokens land closer to $0.37 or to $14.35, and what will each user's speed be?
predict.answer: Much closer to $0.37: step = (16.06 + 16 × 0.157) GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 5.54 ms, so 16 ÷ 5.54 ms ≈ 2,885 tok/s and ≈ $1.04 per million tokens, with each user at ≈ 180 tok/s. Most of the batching win arrives early, because the shared weight read dominates the step until KV reads grow.

apply.task: Build your own lever table from the formula. Using the card's inputs (16.06 GB weights, 0.157 GB KV per 1,200-token request, 3.35 TB/s, $10.8/hr), compute T<sub>step</sub>, total tokens/s, per-user tokens/s and $/M tokens for batch 1, 16 and 64. Then pick an SLO of 6 ms per token and say which of the three batches you can sell.
apply.done: Your table reads roughly 4.79/5.54/7.80 ms, 209/2,885/8,206 tok/s, 209/180/128 tok/s per user and ≈ $14.35/$1.04/$0.37 per M; under a 6 ms SLO, batch 16 is the largest you can sell.
apply.hint: T<sub>step</sub> = (16.06 + B × 0.157) GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s; the math (2 × 8.03e9 × B ÷ 989e12) stays under 1.1 ms, so ignore it.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how fast $/token falls with batch, or how slowly per-user speed drops?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the weight read is shared across users but the KV read isn't?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: batch → step time, or step time → SLO → maximum batch?
Which course on the map do you now most want to open first, and which lever does it serve?
Revisit this card after perf-2: can you rebuild the formula without looking?
